chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
question_text: Give examples of "photosensitive substances". Why are they called so?

verification.note: From FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students, physics section, Ch.12 (printed p.42); the book prints no exam-year citations for this chapter. The 1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Paper-II bank the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Hand-checked physically: the alkali metals sodium, potassium, lithium and caesium have work functions near 2 eV (caesium 2.14 eV), and visible-light photons carry roughly 1.6 to 3.1 eV, so visible light can emit photoelectrons from them — the book's reason (very low work function) is correct. The book's example list also names calcium, zinc, cadmium and magnesium; those respond to ultraviolet rather than visible light, but the list is reproduced as the book prints it. A lecturer's pen tick marks this question in the source scan as one to expect.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.margin_note: First mark. Two or three named metals are enough; the alkali metals are the safest picks.
steps.why: The examiner wants named substances, and the alkali metals head every textbook list because their work functions are the lowest.
common_mistakes: Naming compounds or non-metals. The standard examples are metals.
Giving one example when the question asks for examples. Write at least two.

recall.must_convey: At least two named photosensitive metals, such as sodium, potassium, lithium or caesium.

steps.memory_tip: Start with the alkali metals in order: lithium, sodium, potassium, caesium.

lines.text: Low work function: visible light is enough

steps.margin_note: Second mark. The reason is the low work function; connect it to visible light emitting photoelectrons.
steps.why: A visible photon carries about 1.6 to 3.1 eV. Only a metal whose work function sits at or below this range can emit electrons under visible light, which is why low work function is the whole reason.
common_mistakes: Saying they are sensitive because they are metals. All the examples are metals; the low work function is what sets them apart.
Writing high work function. The work function must be LOW for visible light to be enough.

recall.must_convey: That these substances have a very low work function, so even visible light can make them emit photoelectrons.
accept: light makes them give out electrons

steps.memory_tip: Photo plus sensitive: sensitive even to ordinary visible light, because the work function is low.

insider_note: Examples earn one mark and the reason the other — and the reason must contain the words low work function.
